# Rust from Zero: Ownership, Borrowing and Cargo

Last verified: 2026-10-30 against the Rust Book (ch04, ch09-02, ch10, ch14-01), std `Copy` docs, Cargo Book, cppreference (RAII, `std::move`, object lifetime), Python language reference (data model, simple statements), Go blog "Go Slices: usage and internals", docs.rs `tokio::spawn`; snippets compiled with rustc 1.99.1 on macOS.
Starts from: you can read Python, C++ or Go, and have never written Rust. Builds toward rust-systems/01-async-await-runtime, which opens straight into Tokio and assumes everything here.

## The problem and why it matters

A data-plane service (the part of a system that moves requests and bytes) is written in Rust so that two bugs cannot reach production: using memory after it was freed, and two threads changing the same data at once. Rust checks this at compile time with a few rules.

Expect to argue with the compiler for weeks. Below: the rules, and the real errors for the four mistakes you will make most.

All output below is from `rustc 1.99.1` on an Apple M4 (macOS). Error wording can change between compiler versions.

## First principles

1. **Every value has one owner.** The Rust book: "Each value in Rust has an _owner_." and "There can only be one owner at a time."
2. **When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.** "Rust calls `drop` automatically at the closing curly bracket." No garbage collector.
3. **Assigning or passing a value moves it.** The old name is dead.
4. **To avoid moving, borrow** with a reference: `&T` (read-only) or `&mut T` (read-write).
5. **The borrow rule.** "At any given time, you can have _either_ one mutable reference _or_ any number of immutable references."
6. **References must always be valid.** A reference cannot outlive what it points to.

## How it works

### Move: one owner at a time

A **scope** is the region between `{` and `}` where a name exists. A **move** transfers ownership.

```
  let s1 = String::from("hello");
  +----------+        +-----------+
  | s1 (own) |------->| "hello"   |  heap
  +----------+        +-----------+

  let s2 = s1;      // MOVE
  +----------+        +-----------+
  | s1  dead |   x    | "hello"   |
  +----------+    +-->|           |
  | s2 (own) |----+   +-----------+
  +----------+
  s2 drops at "}" -> buffer freed once
```

If both names stayed valid, both would free the buffer (a double free). The book: "Rust considers `s1` as no longer valid."

For C++ readers: the book itself says `drop` "will be familiar to you if you've used RAII patterns" (RAII: an object's destructor releases its resource when the object's lifetime ends). The difference is the move. In C++ you opt in with `std::move`, which is only a cast to an rvalue reference, and a moved-from standard-library object stays usable in a "valid but unspecified state". In Rust a move is the default and the compiler rejects any later use of the moved-from name.

For Python readers: `b = a` binds a second name to the same object, and both names stay valid. The language reference says objects "may be garbage-collected" once unreachable (CPython uses reference counting). Rust has no collector, so it needs exactly one owner to know when to free.

### Copy versus Clone

Small plain values copy instead of moving. The std docs: `Copy` is for "Types whose values can be duplicated simply by copying bits." Integers, `bool`, floats, `char` and tuples of those qualify. `String` does not: "any type implementing `Drop` can't be `Copy`."

`Clone` is explicit: `x.clone()` can run any code to duplicate, such as a deep copy of heap data. The book: "that code may be expensive."

```rust
let a = String::from("hello");
let b = a.clone(); // deep copy: a and b each own one
let c = b; // move: b is dead after this
let n = 5; // i32 is Copy
let m = n; // n stays usable
```

Compiled and run inside `main` with `println!` of `a`, `c`, `n`, `m` (rustc 1.99.1, Apple M4): `a = hello, c = hello` and `n = 5, m = 5`.

My heuristic: `.clone()` to get unstuck is fine while learning; in a hot path make it a choice.

### Mistake 1: use after move

```rust
fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s1;
    println!("{s1}, world! {s2}");
}
```

Real error (long label re-wrapped by me, `-->` lines and `help` trimmed):

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`
2 |     let s1 = String::from("hello");
  |         -- move occurs because `s1` has type
  |            `String`, which does not implement
  |            the `Copy` trait
3 |     let s2 = s1;
  |              -- value moved here
4 |     println!("{s1}, world! {s2}");
  |                ^^ value borrowed here after move
```

How to read any borrow error: it labels places in line order. Where the value came from, where the first thing happened ("moved here"), where you broke the rule ("after move"). The `help:` is often the fix.

### Borrowing: references

A **reference** lets code use a value without owning it. The borrow rule is a readers-writer lock enforced at compile time:

```
  For one value, at one moment, allowed:

  +-----------------------------------+
  | &T   &T   &T   &T   ...  (readers)|
  +-----------------------------------+
                  OR
  +-----------------------------------+
  | &mut T   (exactly one writer)     |
  +-----------------------------------+

  Never a writer beside a reader,
  never two writers.
```

A **data race** needs "Two or more pointers access the same data at the same time", "At least one of the pointers is being used to write", and "no mechanism being used to synchronize access". The book says Rust "can prevent data races at compile time" by refusing code that has them.

A borrow lasts until its last use, not the end of the scope; hence "later used here" in errors. The book: "a reference's scope starts from where it is introduced and continues through the last time that reference is used."

### Mistake 2: a writer beside a reader

You hold a pointer to the first element of a `Vec` (a growable array), then grow the `Vec`, which can move its buffer.

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let first = &v[0];
    v.push(4);
    println!("first = {first}");
}
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable because
              it is also borrowed as immutable
3 |     let first = &v[0];
  |                  - immutable borrow occurs here
4 |     v.push(4);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
5 |     println!("first = {first}");
  |                        ----- immutable borrow
  |                              later used here
```

Fix: copy the number out (`i32` is `Copy`) so no borrow remains: `let first = v[0];`. Compiled and ran: `first = 1, v = [1, 2, 3, 4]`.

Two writers fail the same way. With `let r1 = &mut s; let r2 = &mut s;` and then a use of `r1`, rustc 1.99.1 says `error[E0499]: cannot borrow `s` as mutable more than once at a time`. Fix: finish with `r1` before creating `r2`; that compiled and printed `hello, world!?`.

### Mistake 3: mutating through `&`

```rust
fn change(some_string: &String) {
    some_string.push_str(", world");
}
```

```
error[E0596]: cannot borrow `*some_string` as mutable,
              as it is behind a `&` reference
(label line trimmed)
help: consider changing this to be a mutable reference
1 | fn change(some_string: &mut String) {
```


Fix: take `&mut String`, declare `let mut s`, call `change(&mut s)`. Both `mut`s are needed. Compiled and ran: `hello, world`.

### Lifetimes, and Mistake 4: returning a reference to a local

A **lifetime** is the span of code in which a reference is valid. The book: "The main aim of lifetimes is to prevent dangling references", meaning references to freed memory. In C++, using an object or reference after its lifetime ended is undefined behaviour (cppreference, object lifetime); in Rust it is a compile error.

```rust
fn shout(x: &str) -> &str {
    let s = x.to_uppercase();
    &s
}
```

```
error[E0515]: cannot return reference to local
              variable `s`
3 |     &s
  |     ^^ returns a reference to data owned by the
  |        current function
```

`s` is dropped at the closing brace, so the reference would dangle. Fix: `fn shout(x: &str) -> String` returning the owned value; it compiled and printed `HI`.

One lifetime signature to recognise (from the book; compiled, printed `service`):

```rust
fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if x.len() > y.len() { x } else { y }
}
```

Read `'a` as "the output is valid no longer than both inputs". The book: annotations "don't change how long any of the references live"; they describe relationships. Skip fancier lifetime syntax until you meet it.

### Strings, Vecs and slices

`String` owns a growable heap buffer; `&str` is a borrowed view of text. `Vec<T>` owns a growable array; `&[T]` is a borrowed view of a run of `T` (a slice).

The book: "A slice is a kind of reference, so it does not have ownership," and string literals have type `&str`. Go slices are also views ("a descriptor of an array segment"; slicing "does not copy the slice's data"), so many can share one array and write through it. Rust slices are references, so they follow the borrow rule: the book's `first_word` example fails with E0502 if you `clear()` the `String` while the slice is still used.

Habit: take `&str` and `&[T]` as parameters; the book says that "makes our API more general". Compiled and run: `first_word(&owned)` gave `hello` and `first_word("literal text")` gave `literal`; `sum(&v)` gave `15` and `sum(&v[1..3])` gave `5` for `v = [1,2,3,4,5]`.

### Option, Result and `?`

A function that may return nothing returns `Option<T>` (`Some(x)` or `None`). A function that may fail returns `Result<T, E>` (`Ok(x)` or `Err(e)`). The compiler makes you handle both.

`?` is the shortcut. The book: on `Ok`, "the value inside the `Ok` will get returned from this expression"; on `Err`, "the `Err` will be returned from the whole function". On an `Option`, `?` is similar: `None` is returned early from the function, `Some(x)` gives `x`.

```rust
fn parse_port(s: &str) -> Result<u16, ParseIntError> {
    let n: u16 = s.trim().parse()?;
    Ok(n)
}
```

Run: `parse_port("8080")` printed `Ok(8080)`; `parse_port("http")` printed `Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })`. A `?` on `m.get(k)` in a function returning `Option<u16>` gave `Some(443) None` for a present and a missing key.

`?` needs a return type that can carry the failure; you "can't mix and match" `Option` and `Result`. In a plain `fn main()`:

```
error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a
function that returns `Result` or `Option` (or another
type that implements `FromResidual`)
```

(First line only.) Fix: `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>` ending in `Ok(())`, as the compiler suggests. `.unwrap()` instead panics (crashes the thread) on `None` or `Err`; prefer `?` in service code.

### Structs, `impl` and traits

A **struct** groups fields; an `impl` block adds methods. The first parameter says how a method borrows: `&self` (read), `&mut self` (write), `self` (consume: a move).

```rust
struct Counter { hits: u32 }
impl Counter {
    fn hit(&mut self) { self.hits += 1 }
    fn total(&self) -> u32 { self.hits }
}
```

A **trait** is a set of methods a type promises to have; the book: "A _trait_ defines the functionality a particular type has and can share with other types." `impl Trait` as a parameter type "accepts any type that implements the specified trait", and is sugar for a trait bound `<T: Trait>`.

```rust
trait Describe { fn describe(&self) -> String; }
impl Describe for Counter {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("at {}", self.hits)
    }
}
fn print_it(x: &impl Describe) {
    println!("{}", x.describe());
}
```

After two `hit()` calls, `total()` printed `2`; `print_it` printed `at 2` (the compiled version said `counter at 2`).

Why it matters next: Tokio signatures carry bounds like `F: Future + Send + 'static`. Read `T: Send` as "T must implement the trait `Send`". What `Send` and `Sync` mean is for rust-systems/05; for now they are bounds the compiler checks.

### Cargo: the build tool

`cargo new demo` creates `Cargo.toml` and `src/main.rs` (the Cargo book shows this tree). On rustc 1.99.1 the generated `[package]` table was `name = "demo"`, `version = "0.1.0"`, `edition = "2024"`,
plus an empty `[dependencies]` table.

Daily commands: `cargo check` (type-check, no final binary), `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo test` (runs `#[test]` functions), `cargo clippy` (lints beyond the compiler), `cargo fmt` (format; `--check` only reports), `cargo build --release`.

The Cargo book: `check` "will essentially compile the packages without performing the final step of code generation, which is faster than running `cargo build`." Use it as your save-key loop.

`cargo build` uses the `dev` profile (a bundle of compiler settings); `--release` uses `release`. The book: "release mode trades longer compile time for code that runs faster." Never benchmark a debug build. Binaries land in `target/debug/` or `target/release/`; I confirmed `target/release/tour` after a release build.

`cargo test` on two `parse_port` tests printed `ok. 2 passed; 0 failed`; `cargo clippy` and `cargo fmt --check` were clean.

Dependencies (crates, i.e. libraries) go under `[dependencies]`. `cargo add itoa` wrote `itoa = "1.0.18"`. The Cargo book: a bare version is a caret requirement, so `"1.2.3"` means `>=1.2.3, <2.0.0`.

## Common mistakes

- **Cloning to silence an error** without asking who should own the value.
- **`&String` or `&Vec<T>` parameters.** Take `&str` and `&[T]`.
- **`.unwrap()` everywhere**, and **benchmarking `cargo run`** (dev profile).

## Try it

About 30 minutes, in a scratch project outside any repo: `cargo new scratch`.

1. Reproduce Mistake 1. Fix it with `.clone()`, then by passing `&s1` to a function taking `&str`. Which is cheaper, and why?
2. Reproduce Mistake 2. Fix it by moving `push` after the last use of `first`.
3. Write `parse_pair(s: &str) -> Result<(i32, i32), std::num::ParseIntError>` (split on a comma, `?` twice) with two `#[test]`s; run `cargo test`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt`.

Done when you can name the first principle behind each error.
